policy_title: Reform student loans and university admissions
stated: Reform UK will scrap interest on student loans, extend loan capital repayment periods to 45 years, restrict undergraduate numbers, and enforce minimum entry standards for universities.

source.quote: Scrap Interest on Student Loans Extend loan capital repayment periods to 45 years. Restrict undergraduate numbers well below current levels, too many courses are not good enough and students are being ripped off. Enforce minimum entry standards.

bearing_set.reason: Restricting undergraduate numbers and enforcing minimum entry standards directly limits access to higher education, while scrapping interest and extending repayment terms materially alters affordability and the attainment gap — all core to education and opportunity.

Abolishing student loan interest reduces the total financial burden on graduate borrowers, directly affecting their real disposable income over the repayment period — a non-negligible cost-of-living effect for the graduate cohort.

Extending capital repayment to 45 years (vs. current 30-year write-off) means lower-earning graduates — those least likely to have cleared their loans — may still be making repayments in their late 50s/early 60s, directly reducing their capacity to save for retirement and raising pensioner-poverty risk.

Scrapping interest reduces the total repayment burden for graduates (who repay 9% of income above threshold via HMRC), directly affecting graduate take-home pay; the 45-year extension runs in the opposite direction for many, making the net effect on disposable income a genuine, non-negligible policy question.

Removing interest on a student loan book exceeding £200bn is a material fiscal cost that widens the gap between receipts and outgoings on the loan book, bearing concretely on debt-path sustainability.

membership_note: Three fundamentals earn real verdicts: access and standards reform lands squarely on O7; the repayment restructuring affects graduate take-home pay (O11); and the interest removal is a non-trivial fiscal subsidy change (O12). Distributional effects on inequality (O14) are real but captured within O7's attainment-gap indicator rather than warranting a separate O14 bearing, as the mechanism runs through educational access rather than income/wealth redistribution directly.
